source_text: Tempus est his decursis repetere nos de incarnatione domini et salvatoris nostri, quomodo vel homo factus est vel inter homines conversatus est. Pro viribus igitur nostris perexiguis considerata ex operum suorum magis quam ex nostri sensus contemplatione divina natura, intuitisque nihilominus creaturis eius visibilibus, fide quoque invisibilibus contemplatis, quia non omnia vel oculis videre potest humana fragilitas vel ratione conplecti, pro eo quod omnium rationabilium infirmius et fragilius animal nos sumus homines (praestantiora enim sunt ea, quae vel in caelo vel super caelos habentur): superest ut harum omnium creaturarum et dei medium, id est -mediatoremquaeramus, quem Paulus apostolus “primogenitum omnis creaturaepronuntiat. Videntes quoque nos ea, quae de eius maiestate in seripturis sanctis referuntur, et intuentes quod “imago invisibilis deie et “primogenitus omnis creaturae” dicatur, et quod “in ipso creata sunt omnia visibilia et invisibilia, sive throni sive dominationes sive principatus sive potestates, omnia per ipsum et in ipso creata sunt, et ipse est ante omnes, et omnia illi constant”, qui est “caput omnium”, solus habens “capute deum patrem, sicut seriptum est: “Caput autem Christi deus”; pervidentes etiam quod scriptum est quoniam “nemo novit patrem nisi filius, neque filium quis novit nisi pater” (quis enim potest nosse quae sib “sapientia- nisl qui genuit eam? aut quis ad liquidum quae sit ‘veritas’ novit nisi veritatis pater? quis certe universam -“verbi” sul naturam atque ipsius “dei- quae ex deo est investigare potuit nisi solus deus, -apud quem erat verbum-?): pro certo habere debemus quod hoc verbum (sive ratio dicenda est) hane sapientiam, hane veritatem nullus alius “nisi solus pater novit, de quo seriptum est: “Ne ipsum quidem mundum capere arbitror libros qui scriberentur”, de gloria scilicet et maiestate filu dei. Inpossibile namque est litteris committere ea, quae ad salvatoris gloriam pertinent. His igitur tantis ac talibus de natura filü dei consideratis, cum summa ammiratione obstupescimus quod eminens omnium ista natura ‘exinaniens’ se de statu maiestatis suae homo factus sit et inter homines conversatus sit, sicut gratia labiis eius infusa- testatur, et sicut ei testimonium reddit pater caelestis, et ut signis quoque et prodigus variisque ab eo gestis virtutibus confirmatur. Qui etiam ante praesentiam suam hane, quam ostendit in corpore, praecursores et nuntios adventus sui misit prophetas; post ascensionem vero suam in caelos sanctos apostolos divinitatis suae virtute repletos homines vel ex publicanis vel ex piseatoribus imperitos et indoctos ceircumire fecit orbem terrarum, ut ex omni gente atque ex omnibus populis piorum plebem in se credentium congregarent. 2. Verum ex omnibus de eo miraculis et magnificis illud. penitus ammirationem humanae mentis excedit, nec invenit mortalis intellegentiae fragilitas, quomodo sentire vel intellegere possit quod tanta illa potentia divinae maiestatis, ipsum illud patris verbum atque ipsa sapientia dei, in qua “creata sunt omnia visibilia et invisibilia, intra eireumseriptionem eius hominis, qui apparuit in Iudaea, fuisse credenda sit, sed et ingressa esse dei sapientia vulvam feminae et nasci parvulus et vagitum emittere ad similitudinem plorantium parvulorum; tum deinde quod et in morte conturbari refertur, ut ipse etiam profitetur dicens: “Tristis est anima mea usque ad mortem”; et ad ultimum quod usque ad eam quae inter homines indignissima habetur adductus est mortem, licet post tertiam surrexerit diem. Cum ergo quaedam in eo ita videamus humana, ut nihil a communi mortalium fragihtate distare videantur, quaedam ita divina, quae nulli alii nisi illi primae et ineffabili naturae conveniant deitatis, haeret humani intellectus angustia et tantae ammirationis stupore pereulsa, quo declinet, quid teneat, quo se convertat, ignorat. Si deum sentiat, mortalem videt; si hominem putet, devicto "mortis regno cum spoliüs redeuntem a mortuis cernit. Propter quod cum omni metu et reverentia contemplandum est, ut in uno eodemque ita utriusque naturae veritas demonstretur, ut neque aliquid indignum et indecens in divina illa et ineffabili substantia sentiatur, neque rursum quae gesta sunt falsis inlusa imaginibus aestimentur. Quae quidem in aures humanas proferre et sermonibus explicare, longe vires vel meriti nostri vel ingenii ac sermonis excedit. Arbitror autem quia etiam sanctorum apostolorum supergrediatur mensuram; quin immo fortassis etiam totius creaturae caelestium virtutum eminentior est saeramenti istius explanatio. De quo nos non temeritate aliqua, sed quoniam ordo loci poposcit, ea magis quae fides nostra continet, quam quae humanae rationis adsertio vindicare solet, quam paucissimis proferemus, suspiciones potius nostras quam manifestas aliquas adfirmationes in medium proferentes. 3. lgitur unigenitus filius dei, per quem ‘omnia facta esse visibilia et invisibilia- in superioribus sermo disputationis edocuit, secundum seripturae sententiam et fecit omnia et “quae fecit diligit. Nam cum ‘invisibilis dei’ ipse sit -imago- invisibilis, participationem sui universis rationabilibus creaturis invisibiliter praebuit ita, ut tantum ex eo unusquisque participi sumeret, quanto erga eum dilectionis inhaesisset adfectu. Verum cum pro liberi arbitri facultate varietas unumquemque ae diversitas habuisset animorum, ut alius ardentiore, alius tenuiore et exiliore erga auctorem suum amore teneretur, illa anima, de qua dixit lesus quia “nemo aufert a me animam meam”, ab initio creaturae et deinceps inseparabiliter ei atque indissociabihter inhaerens, utpote sapientiae et verbo dei et veritati ac luci verae, et tota totum recipiens atque in eius lucem splendoremque ipsa cedens, facta est cum ipso principaliter unus spiritus, sicut et apostolus his, qui eam imitari deberent, promittit, quia “qui se iungit domino, unus spiritus este. Hac ergo substantia animae inter deum carnemque mediante (mon enim possibile erat dei naturam corpori sine mediatore misceri) nascitur, ut diximus, deus-homo, illa substantia media existente, cui utique contra naturam non erat corpus assumere. Sed neque rursum anima illa, utpote substantia rationabilis, contra naturam habuit capere deum, in quem, ui superius diximus, velut (m) verbum sapienti tatem tota iam cesserai. Unde et mero pro eo quod vel tota esset in fiho dei vel totum in se caperet f dei. eiiam ipsa cum ea quam assumserat carne dei filius dei virtus, Christus et dei sapiemiis ap- B pellatur; rursum dei filius, ‘per quem ommia creata sunt4 lesus Christus et; fius hominmis nomunatur. Nam et filius dei mortuus esse dieiur, pro ea seilicet natura, quae mortem wiique reeipere poterx et filus hominis appellatur, qui ‘venturus im dei patris gloria eum sanctis angelis- praedicatur. Et hae de per ommem seripturam -10 tam divina natura humanis vocabulis appellatur, quam humana natur divinae nuncupaiionis insignibus decoratur. Magis de hoe quam de ullo alio diei potest quod seriptum esi quia “erunt: ambo im earme una, et iam non sunt duo, sed earo una”. Magis enim verbum dei eum anima in carne una- esse, quam vir eum uxore putandus est. Sed et -unus spiritus- esse cum deo cui eonvenit quam hum animae. quae se ita deo per dilectionem iunxit, uf eo unus Spiritus merrio dieatur? Quod autem dilectionis en meri siisckn ndn "ete: ei inseparabilem cum deo fecerit unitatem, iia ut mom forítura fuent aui eum personae aeceptione animae eius assumptüio, sed virtutum — suarum ei merito delata, audi ad eam prophetam dicentem: “Dilexisti - iuslitüiam et; odisii iniquitatem; propterea unxit te deus, deus tuus oleo laetitiae prae participibus tuis”. Dilectionis igitur merito unguitur ‘oleo laetitiae, id est anima cum verbo dei Christus efficitur. -Unginamque ‘oleo laetitiae- non aliud intellegitur quam spiritu sancto repleri. Quod autem “prae participibus- dixit, indicat quia non gratia spiritus sicut prophetis ei data est, sed ipsius verbi dei in ea substantialis inerat “plenitudo”, sicut et apostolus dixit: “In quo inhabitat omnis plenitudo deitatis corporahter”. Denique propter hoe non solum dixit: “Dilexisti iustitiam”, sed addidit “et odisti iniquitatem”. ‘Odisse- enim ‘iniquitatem- illud est, quod scriptura dicit de eo quia “peccatum non fecit, nec inventus est dolus in ore eius”, et quod ait: “Temptatus per omnia pro similitudine absque peccato”. Sed et ipse dominus dicit: “Quis vestrum me arguit de peccato?” Et iterum ipse dicit de se: “Eece venit mundi huius princeps et in me non invenit quidquam”. Quae omnia nullum in eo peccati sensum indicant extitisse. Quod ut propheta evidentius designaret, quia numquam eum -iniquitatis- sensus intrasset, ait: “Priusquam sciret puer vocare patrem aut matrem, avertit se ab iniquitate”.
thought_title: Incarnation of the Lord and Savior
pass_a_gloss: It is time, having gone through these things, to repeat concerning the incarnation of our Lord and Savior, how he was made man or lived among men. Therefore, having considered, according to our weak powers, more from the contemplation of his works than from our own sense, and having intuited, nevertheless, his visible creatures, and also having contemplated his invisible ones by faith, because human fragility is not able to see all things with the eyes or to comprehend them with reason, and because we men are the weakest and most fragile of all rational animals (for those things that are in heaven or above the heavens are more excellent), it remains that we seek the medium of all these creatures and of God, that is, the mediator, whom Paul the apostle pronounces as the firstborn of all creation. Seeing also those things that are referred to in the holy scriptures concerning his majesty, and intuited that he is said to be the image of the invisible God and the firstborn of all creation, and that all visible and invisible things were created in him, and that he is before all things, and that all things consist in him, who is the head of all things, having only God the Father as his head, as it is written: The head of Christ is God, foreseeing also that which is written, that no one knows the Father except the Son, nor does anyone know the Son except the Father (for who can know what wisdom is, except the one who begot it? or who can know what truth is, except the Father of truth? who, certainly, can investigate the nature of the Word, which is from God, except God alone, in whom the Word was?), we ought to hold for certain that this Word (or reason) knows this wisdom, this truth, no one else except the only Father, about whom it is written: I do not think that the world itself could contain the books that would be written, concerning the glory and majesty of the Son of God. For it is impossible to commit to writing those things that pertain to the glory of the Savior. Having considered, therefore, these great and such things concerning the nature of the Son of God, we are astonished with the greatest admiration that this eminent nature, above all things, emptied itself, having become man, and lived among men, as the grace poured into his lips testifies, and as the heavenly Father bears witness to him, and as it is confirmed by the signs and various prodigies and virtues done by him. He also sent prophets, precursors and heralds of his coming, before his presence, which he showed in the body; and after his ascension into the heavens, he made holy apostles, filled with the virtue of his divinity, men who were formerly publicans or fishermen, unskilled and uneducated, to go around the circle of the earth, so that from every nation and from all peoples they might gather a multitude of the pious, believing in him. But of all the miracles and magnificent things concerning him, that which exceeds the admiration of the human mind and does not find the fragility of mortal intelligence, is how that great power of divine majesty, the very Word of the Father and the wisdom of God, in whom all visible and invisible things were created, is believed to have been enclosed within the circumscription of that man who appeared in Judea, but also to have entered the womb of a woman and to have been born as a little child and to have emitted a cry, like that of crying children; then, also, that he is said to have been troubled even unto death, as he himself also professes, saying: My soul is sorrowful even unto death; and, finally, that he was led to that death, which is considered the most ignominious among men, although he rose again on the third day. When, therefore, we see certain things in him in a human way, so that they do not seem to differ from the common fragility of mortals, and certain things in a divine way, which are fitting to no one else except that first and ineffable nature of divinity, the narrowness of the human intellect is stuck and, overcome by the stupor of such great admiration, it does not know what to hold, where to turn, or what to do. If it senses God, it sees a mortal; if it thinks of a man, it sees one who, having conquered the kingdom of death, returns from the dead with spoils. On account of which, it ought to be contemplated with all fear and reverence, so that in one and the same thing the truth of both natures may be demonstrated, so that nothing unworthy or unseemly may be sensed in that divine and ineffable substance, nor, on the other hand, may the things that were done be estimated as false and imaginary. Which things, indeed, to bring forth into human ears and to explain in speeches, far exceed the powers or merits or genius or speech of ours. I think, however, that even the minds of the holy apostles surpass this; nay, perhaps even the explanation of this sacrament is more excellent than that of all the celestial virtues. Concerning which, we shall bring forth a few things, not with any temerity, but because the order of the place has demanded it, rather what our faith contains than what the assertion of human reason is accustomed to vindicate, putting forth our suspicions rather than manifest affirmations. The only-begotten Son of God, through whom all visible and invisible things were made, as the scripture says, and who made all things and loves what he made, since he himself is the image of the invisible God, invisibly gave a participation of himself to all rational creatures, so that each one might participate in him to the extent that he had adhered to him with love. But when, on account of the faculty of free will, a variety and diversity of souls had occurred, so that one was held by a more ardent love, another by a more tenuous and slender love towards his author, that soul, concerning which Jesus said that no one takes away my soul from me, from the beginning of creation and afterwards, inseparably and indissolubly adhered to him, as it were, to the wisdom and Word of God and to the truth and light, and receiving all things in all, and yielding itself to his light and splendor, became one spirit with him, as the apostle promises to those who ought to imitate it, saying: He who is joined to the Lord is one spirit. Therefore, by this substance of the soul, which is the medium between God and flesh (for it was not possible for the nature of God to be mixed with the body without a mediator), the God-man is born, as we have said, with this medium substance existing, to which, indeed, it was not against nature to assume a body. But neither did that soul, as a rational substance, have against nature to receive God, into whom, as we said above, it had already entirely yielded, as it were, to the Word of wisdom. Whence, also, on account of this, that it was all in the Son of God or that it had received all of God, the Son of God, with the flesh that he had assumed, is called Christ, and the power of God, and the wisdom of God; and, again, the Son of God, through whom all things were created, is called Jesus Christ, and the Son of man. For the Son of God is said to have died, on account of that nature which was able to receive death, and the Son of man is called the one who is to come in the glory of God the Father with the holy angels. And these things are called, throughout the whole scripture, both the divine nature with human words, and the human nature with the insignia of divine appellation. It can be said more concerning this than concerning any other thing, that which is written: They shall be two in one flesh, and they are no longer two, but one flesh. For the Word of God is more to be believed to be one with the soul in the flesh than a man with his wife. But also to be one spirit with God is fitting to the human soul, which has joined itself to God through love, so that it may be said to be one spirit, merited by love. But what is the merit of love, if it has made an inseparable unity with God, so that there is not a separation of persons, but a reception of virtues, as the prophet says to him: You have loved justice and hated iniquity; therefore, God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness beyond your companions. Therefore, the merit of love is anointed with the oil of gladness, that is, the soul with the Word of God becomes Christ. And to be anointed with the oil of gladness is understood as being filled with the Holy Spirit. But when it is said: beyond your companions, it indicates that it is not the grace of the Spirit, as it was given to the prophets, but the fullness of the Word of God, which was substantially in it, as the apostle said: In whom all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily. Finally, on account of this, it is not only said: You have loved justice, but it is added: and hated iniquity. For to hate iniquity is that which the scripture says concerning him, that he did not commit sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth, and that he was tempted in all things, like us, without sin. And the Lord himself says: Which of you convicts me of sin? And again, he says concerning himself: Behold, the prince of this world comes, and in me he finds nothing. All these things indicate that there was no sense of sin in him. Which thing the prophet more evidently designated, saying: Before the child knows how to call father or mother, he turned away from iniquity.

pass_b_english: The time has come, now that we have passed through these matters, to return to the incarnation of our Lord and Savior—how he became man and lived among us. We consider this according to our very limited powers, drawing more from the contemplation of his works than from our own understanding. We have observed his visible creatures and, by faith, contemplated the invisible ones as well, since human frailty cannot see everything with the eyes or grasp everything by reason. We human beings are, after all, the weakest and most fragile of all rational animals, for those beings that exist in heaven or above the heavens are far more excellent. Therefore we must seek the mediator between all these creatures and God, the very one whom the apostle Paul calls the firstborn of all creation (Colossians 1:15). We see what the holy scriptures say of his majesty: that he is the image of the invisible God and the firstborn of all creation (Colossians 1:15); that in him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities (Colossians 1:16); that he is before all things and in him all things hold together (Colossians 1:17); that he is the head of all things, having God the Father alone as his head, as it is written: "The head of Christ is God" (1 Corinthians 11:3). We also perceive that no one knows the Father except the Son, and no one knows the Son except the Father (Matthew 11:27; Luke 10:22). For who can know what wisdom is except the one who begot it? Who can know what truth is except the Father of truth? Who could explore the nature of the Word that is from God except God alone, in whom the Word was? (John 1:1) We must therefore hold it certain that this Word—or Reason, if you prefer—knows this wisdom and this truth, and that no one but the Father knows them. As it is written: "I do not think the world itself could contain the books that would be written" (John 21:25), concerning the glory and majesty of the Son of God. It is impossible to commit to writing what pertains to the Savior's glory. Having considered these great and stupendous things about the nature of the Son of God, we stand astonished with the utmost wonder that this supreme nature emptied itself, becoming man and living among men. The grace poured upon his lips testifies to this (Psalm 45:2), the heavenly Father bears witness to him (Matthew 3:17; 17:5), and it is confirmed by the signs, diverse wonders, and mighty works he performed. He also sent prophets as forerunners and heralds of his coming before he appeared in the body. After his ascension into the heavens, he filled holy apostles with the power of his divinity—men who were formerly tax collectors or fishermen, unskilled and uneducated—and sent them around the whole earth so that from every nation and all peoples they might gather a community of the godly who believe in him.

Yet of all his miracles and mighty deeds, this one utterly surpasses the wonder of the human mind; the frailty of mortal intelligence cannot find how to conceive it: that the very Word of the Father and the Wisdom of God, in whom all visible and invisible things were created (Colossians 1:16), is believed to have been enclosed within the bodily limits of the man who appeared in Judea. Not only that, but that the Wisdom of God entered a woman's womb, was born as an infant, and cried like any other child. Then, too, he is said to have been troubled even to the point of death, as he himself declared: "My soul is sorrowful even to death" (Matthew 26:38). Finally, he was brought to the most shameful death known among men, even though he rose again on the third day. When we see certain things in him that are so human they seem no different from the common frailty of mortals, and other things so divine that they belong only to that first, ineffable divine nature, the narrowness of human intellect is stopped short, overwhelmed by the stupor of such wonder. It does not know what to hold, where to turn, or what to do. If it senses God, it sees a mortal; if it thinks him a man, it sees one who, having conquered the kingdom of death, returns from the dead bearing spoils (Ephesians 4:8; Colossians 2:15). Therefore he must be contemplated with all fear and reverence, so that in one and the same person the truth of both natures may be shown—so that nothing unworthy or unseemly is attributed to that divine and ineffable substance, nor, on the other hand, are the things he did dismissed as false or imaginary. To set these things forth to human ears and explain them in words far exceeds our powers, our merits, our genius, or our speech. I suspect it even surpasses the minds of the holy apostles; indeed, perhaps the explanation of this mystery is more excellent than that of all the heavenly powers. Concerning this, we will set forth only a few things, not out of rashness, but because the order of our subject demands it—drawing from what our faith contains rather than what human reason usually defends, offering our conjectures rather than dogmatic assertions.

The only-begotten Son of God, through whom all visible and invisible things were made (John 1:3; Colossians 1:16), as scripture teaches, made all things and loves what he made. Since he is himself the image of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15), he invisibly gave a share of himself to all rational creatures, so that each might participate in him to the degree that it clung to him with love. But because of the faculty of free will, a variety and diversity of souls arose: some held fast to their Creator with more ardent love, others with a thinner, weaker love. That soul about which Jesus said, "No one takes my soul from me" (John 10:18), from the beginning of creation and ever after, clung to him inseparably and indissolubly—as to the Wisdom, the Word, the Truth, and the true Light of God—receiving everything from him entirely and yielding itself wholly to his light and splendor. It became one spirit with him principally, just as the apostle promises to those who should imitate it: "He who is joined to the Lord is one spirit" (1 Corinthians 6:17). By this substance of the soul, then, serving as mediator between God and flesh (for it was not possible for the divine nature to unite with a body without a mediator), the God-man is born, as we said, with this mediating substance in place—a substance for which assuming a body was not contrary to nature. Nor was it contrary to the nature of that rational soul to receive God, into whom, as we said above, it had already surrendered itself completely, as it were to the Word of Wisdom. Therefore, because it was wholly in the Son of God, or had received all of God within itself, the Son of God, together with the flesh he assumed, is called Christ, the Power of God, and the Wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24). Again, the Son of God, through whom all things were created, is called Jesus Christ; and he is called the Son of Man. For the Son of God is said to have died, on account of that nature which could undergo death; and the Son of Man is the one who is to come in the glory of God the Father with the holy angels (Matthew 16:27; 25:31). Throughout all scripture, the divine nature is spoken of with human words, and the human nature is adorned with the titles of divinity. One can say more about this than about anything else: what is written, "The two shall become one flesh, and they are no longer two but one flesh" (Genesis 2:24; Ephesians 5:31), is more truly realized in the Word of God being one with the soul in the flesh than in a man and his wife. And to be one spirit with God is fitting for the human soul that has joined itself to God through love, so that it may be said to be one spirit by merit of love. What is the merit of love? It has forged an inseparable unity with God, so that the assumption of the soul was not by a mixture of persons but by the reception of virtues—as the prophet says to him: "You have loved justice and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness beyond your companions" (Psalm 45:7). By merit of love, then, the soul is anointed with the oil of gladness—that is, the soul with the Word of God becomes Christ. To be anointed with the oil of gladness means to be filled with the Holy Spirit. The phrase "beyond your companions" shows that this was not the grace of the Spirit as given to the prophets, but the fullness of the Word of God dwelling substantially in him, as the apostle said: "In him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily" (Colossians 2:9). Finally, for this reason it says not only "You have loved justice" but adds "and hated iniquity." To hate iniquity is what scripture says of him: he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth (1 Peter 2:22; Isaiah 53:9), and he was tempted in every way as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15). The Lord himself says: "Which of you convicts me of sin?" (John 8:46), and again: "Behold, the ruler of this world comes, and he has nothing in me" (John 14:30). All these things show that no sense of sin ever existed in him. To make this even clearer, the prophet says: "Before the child knows how to call father or mother, he turns away from iniquity" (Isaiah 7:16).

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex theological arguments of the Latin text. All scripture citations in Pass B correspond to the Latin text and the context of the quotes (e.g., Colossians 1:15-17, 1 Cor 11:3, Matt 11:27, John 1:1, John 21:25, Psalm 45:2, Matt 3:17, Matt 26:38, 1 Cor 6:17, 1 Cor 1:24, Gen 2:24, Psalm 45:7, Col 2:9, 1 Pet 2:22, Isa 53:9, Heb 4:15, John 8:46, John 14:30, Isa 7:16). The distinction between the soul's participation and the person of Christ is preserved. The translator correctly identified the 'exinaniens' (emptied himself) and 'oleo laetitiae' (oil of gladness) nuances.

source: 'tempus est his decursis repetere nos de incarnatione domini et salvatoris nostri, quomodo vel homo factus est vel inter homines conversatus est.' english: 'It is time, having gone through these things, to repeat concerning the incarnation of our Lord and Savior, how he was made man or lived among men.' source: 'quod “imago invisibilis deie et “primogenitus omnis creaturae” dicatur, et quod “in ipso creata sunt omnia visibilia et invisibilia, sive throni sive dominationes sive principatus sive potestates, omnia per ipsum et in ipso creata sunt, et ipse est ante omnes, et omnia illi constant”, qui est “caput omnium”, solus habens “capute deum patrem, sicut seriptum est: “Caput autem Christi deus”;' english: 'that he is said to be the image of the invisible God and the firstborn of all creation, and that all visible and invisible things were created in him, and that he is before all things, and that all things consist in him, who is the head of all things, having only God the Father as his head, as it is written: The head of Christ is God.'
